author: Yasunari Kawabata
introFa: کتاب «The Old Capital» نوشته Yasunari Kawabata یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Old Capital»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

REVIEWS 215 ing, this approach overlooks other potential explanations and risks generalizations. In the case of Taylor, the fact that he also made stops at India and Japan but formed drastically different opinions of the three lands is not dealt with in much detail. Haddads analysis would have been more complete had more attention been paid to the broader historical and social background under which some of these literatures were produced. Nevertheless, Haddads book marks an important intervention in the critique of conventional orientalism and situates itself in the scholarly stream of revisionist critique of the assumption of a monolithic West. The presentation of multiple points of views offers readers new understand ings of how those in America viewed China in the historical period specified. It also provides sufficient fresh theorization and captivating narrative to interest both the serious scholar and the casual reader. The University of Hong Kong Isaac Yue i Stuart Creighton Miller, The Unwelcome Immigrant: The American Image of the Chinese, 1785-1882 (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1969), p. 104. Gudu xinmao: qiandu hou dao kangzhan qian de Beiping chengshi xiaofei 故都新貌：遷都後 到抗戰前的北平城市消費（i928-i937) [The Old Capital in a New Guise: Market Consumerism after Moving the Capital South to the Beginning of the War of Resistance against Japan [1928 1937]) by Hsu Hui-chi (Xu Huiqi 許慧琦)• Taipei: Xuesheng shuju 學生書局，2008. Preface x，478 pp. nt$66o00 (hardcover), nt$56o00 (paperback), isbn 978-9-5715-1438-3 (hardcover), 978-9-5715-1437-6 (paperback). From 1928 to 1937 the great city of Beijing ；)匕京 was humbled when its name was changed to Beiping 北平.The Nationalist Party (Guomindang 國民黨，hereafter GMD) took control of the central government in 1928 at the end of their military Northern Expedition, moved the capital south to Nanjing 南京 and changed the former capitals name. When invading Japanese troops took north China in 1937, they revived the name Beijing. Beiping began 1928 already on a downward economic spiral. The fall of the Manchus in 1911 meant that the handicraft artisans, custom tailors and outfitters, all those who served the city's wealthy elite, began to lose their sources of income as the Manchu nobles fell on increasingly hard times. The city lost its economic, market and consumer base, and its position as a consumer of luxury items for the Manchu power-holders. When the GMD moved the capital to the south, Beiping no longer had a central role to play in the nations economic life. Large amounts of funds from taxes and government projects no longer flowed through the city, so the investment banks and insurance firms which had managed government funds moved south to Shanghai 上海 or This content downloaded from 130.209.6.61 on Fri, 26 Feb 2016 20:24:52 UTC All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

216 REVIEWS Nanjing, where they could be closer to the revenue flows, and their well-paid managers moved with them. The layers of bureaucrats who had formerly administered government affairs, and even the followers of various now-weakened northern warlords, no longer had jobs in Beiping. The sundry merchants who had supplied the families of the bureaucrats and administrators could not stay in business when their volume of business decreased. Many people in the city experienced a rapid loss of income and status. Hsu Hui-chis book The Old Capital in a New Guise describes the city during the decade it was called Beiping. She talks about the transformations that took place when economic conditions changed, such as the continuing trend of Western modernization and the emergence of new consumers. Hsu shows how large daily markets and temple fairs developed as the most popular places for the sale and exchange of goods. There were large markets at Dongan shichang 東安 市場 and at Tianqiao 天橋，and a number of colourful temple fairs in the city. This manner of selling accommodated the smaller merchants who, because of the poor economy, had fewer goods to sell and could expect fewer customers able to buy something. A simple stall was easy to set up at a temple fair and easy to take down when not in use, all done with minimal cost. This way of selling goods and services was aimed at the middle and lower classes who had almost no discretionary income yet were able to participate in a lively exchange of goods and services, often in the entertaining carnival atmosphere of a temple fair. Among the new institutions that spread in Beiping during this time were public parks, movie houses, swimming pools, dance halls, coffee shops, fruit parlors, massage salons, photo studios, beauty shops, hotels and apartment buildings. The new institutions fostered Western ways of thinking, behaving and dressing. People interacting with the new institutions tended to prefer Western styles of dress, and both males and females moved away from traditional Qing 清 dy nasty (1636-1912) clothing, footwear and hairstyles. Hsu uses these points to describe the rise during the Beiping decade of the professional hostess {nüzhaodai 女招待).Many of these new institutions, she explains, employed women. This provided a new economic opportunity for females to find a job and earn money outside of the home, but it also meant that these females would be in contact with male customers. That was a departure from traditional mores that did not allow males and females to mingle freely or to interact in unsupervised situations. The females who worked in these new institutions were natives of the city, often Manchu girls from families that had become destitute. The girls all had legitimate jobs in these businesses and were officially not there solely to provide sexual services, but generally the selling of their sexual serv ices became their main source of income. Commercial sex could be obtained at all of the new institutions, and shops began advertising the beauty of their female sales clerks. In a city where most incomes were low, who were the customers wanting to meet the host esses? Among their regular customers were the writers, public intellectuals and university professors who worked in the city. As the economy of Beiping deteriorated for most people, the men in these categories continued to enjoy a steady source of income. In fact, as prices fell, their regular salaries bought ever more goods and services. They were easily able to afford attending This content downloaded from 130.209.6.61 on Fri, 26 Feb 2016 20:24:52 UTC All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

REVIEWS 217 the theatre, travelling to visit temples and scenic spots, partaking in lavish restaurant meals, and spending their days buying books and collecting antiques. Removing the hassles and pressures of government business from the city allowed daily life for this category of Beiping citizens to become easier and more relaxed. A further category of customers for the hostesses were young university students. Often com ing from wealthy families, they also enjoyed steady incomes and so had a great advantage over the majority of people whose incomes were catch-as-catch-can. These boys liked to move into the newly constructed apartment buildings, where they could rent a room and live a life virtu ally free of parental or societal strictures. They came to like movies, Western-style haircuts and clothing, imported dance music, and the easy availability of the young female hostesses. In fact, the girl hostesses and their student customers were often very close in age and shared similar interests in new fashion, Western food and jazz. Had they been in a Western city, people would have assumed they were boyfriend and girlfriend out on the town for a carefree evening. Hostesses were able to earn high incomes by catering to many men, and the income of the best hostesses was equal to that of a well-paid professor. Hsu tells us that female hostesses and their male student customers, because both enjoyed strong buying power in a weak market, be came the main drivers of the city's economy during these years. They became the "new consumer’’ who was Western-oriented, young, affluent, and willing to spend. They helped to stimulate the introduction of new ideas, fashions, clothing and furniture imported from abroad. Hsu provides a number of interesting details about the lives of the hostesses. The economic rewards were high, but they entailed, besides the actual sex provided, demeaning acts such as "holdings hands, listening to bad jokes, and telling ones age". Men dissatisfied with one girl might crassly yell out that they wanted another hostess sent over. Males had all sorts of ways of taking maximum advantage of (eating, chi 吃）the poor hostesses. On the other hand, when the girls customer was an inexperienced young college boy, the girl as able to "eat" the boy. For many of the young hostesses, their best friends were the male hustlers (nanzhaodai 男招待)，who shared a similar economic position and faced the same job-related pressures. I hope that in the future Hsu will do more research into this aspect of Beiping life. Hsu describes the intellectual and cultural vibrancy of this decade. The writers and profes sors in the city began to create an industry for the appreciation of old Beijing. Hsu says that the removal of the governmental institutions, and the national gaze from Beiping, allowed its long history and many monuments to rise to the surface of public appreciation. Magazine and news paper writers started to write about the city's distinctive cuisine, its colourful colloquialisms, and its dusty temples and neighbourhood lanes (hutong 胡同）• They were creating a nostalgia for a past that was still within living memory for most citizens. They were also fostering the com mercial tourism that today is a major industry for the city. Hsu presents seventeen tables of information about wages, prices, daily costs of living and population changes during the decade. But her study is as much about Beipings social and cul tural changes as the changes in its market consumerism. From 1928 to 1937 the great city of Beijing ；)匕京 was humbled when its name was changed to Beiping 北平.The Nationalist Party (Guomindang 國民黨，hereafter GMD) took control of the central government in 1928 at the end of their military Northern Expedition, moved the capital south to Nanjing 南京 and changed the former capitals name. When invading Japanese troops took north China in 1937, they revived the name Beijing. Beiping began 1928 already on a downward economic spiral. The fall of the Manchus in 1911 meant that the handicraft artisans, custom tailors and outfitters, all those who served the city's wealthy elite, began to lose their sources of income as the Manchu nobles fell on increasingly hard times. The city lost its economic, market and consumer base, and its position as a consumer of luxury items for the Manchu power-holders. When the GMD moved the capital to the south, Beiping no longer had a central role to play in the nations economic life. Large amounts of funds from taxes and government projects no longer flowed through the city, so the investment banks and insurance firms which had managed government funds moved south to Shanghai 上海 or This content downloaded from 130.209.6.61 on Fri, 26 Feb 2016 20:24:52 UTC All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

216 REVIEWS Nanjing, where they could be closer to the revenue flows, and their well-paid managers moved with them. The layers of bureaucrats who had formerly administered government affairs, and even the followers of various now-weakened northern warlords, no longer had jobs in Beiping. The sundry merchants who had supplied the families of the bureaucrats and administrators could not stay in business when their volume of business decreased. Many people in the city experienced a rapid loss of income and status. Hsu Hui-chis book The Old Capital in a New Guise describes the city during the decade it was called Beiping. She talks about the transformations that took place when economic conditions changed, such as the continuing trend of Western modernization and the emergence of new consumers. Hsu shows how large daily markets and temple fairs developed as the most popular places for the sale and exchange of goods. There were large markets at Dongan shichang 東安 市場 and at Tianqiao 天橋，and a number of colourful temple fairs in the city. This manner of selling accommodated the smaller merchants who, because of the poor economy, had fewer goods to sell and could expect fewer customers able to buy something. A simple stall was easy to set up at a temple fair and easy to take down when not in use, all done with minimal cost. This way of selling goods and services was aimed at the middle and lower classes who had almost no discretionary income yet were able to participate in a lively exchange of goods and services, often in the entertaining carnival atmosphere of a temple fair. Among the new institutions that spread in Beiping during this time were public parks, movie houses, swimming pools, dance halls, coffee shops, fruit parlors, massage salons, photo studios, beauty shops, hotels and apartment buildings. The new institutions fostered Western ways of thinking, behaving and dressing. People interacting with the new institutions tended to prefer Western styles of dress, and both males and females moved away from traditional Qing 清 dy nasty (1636-1912) clothing, footwear and hairstyles. Hsu uses these points to describe the rise during the Beiping decade of the professional hostess {nüzhaodai 女招待).Many of these new institutions, she explains, employed women. This provided a new economic opportunity for females to find a job and earn money outside of the home, but it also meant that these females would be in contact with male customers. That was a departure from traditional mores that did not allow males and females to mingle freely or to interact in unsupervised situations. The females who worked in these new institutions were natives of the city, often Manchu girls from families that had become destitute. The girls all had legitimate jobs in these businesses and were officially not there solely to provide sexual services, but generally the selling of their sexual serv ices became their main source of income. Commercial sex could be obtained at all of the new institutions, and shops began advertising the beauty of their female sales clerks. In a city where most incomes were low, who were the customers wanting to meet the host esses? Among their regular customers were the writers, public intellectuals and university professors who worked in the city. As the economy of Beiping deteriorated for most people, the men in these categories continued to enjoy a steady source of income. In fact, as prices fell, their regular salaries bought ever more goods and services. They were easily able to afford attending This content downloaded from 130.209.6.61 on Fri, 26 Feb 2016 20:24:52 UTC All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

REVIEWS 217 the theatre, travelling to visit temples and scenic spots, partaking in lavish restaurant meals, and spending their days buying books and collecting antiques. Removing the hassles and pressures of government business from the city allowed daily life for this category of Beiping citizens to become easier and more relaxed. A further category of customers for the hostesses were young university students. Often com ing from wealthy families, they also enjoyed steady incomes and so had a great advantage over the majority of people whose incomes were catch-as-catch-can. These boys liked to move into the newly constructed apartment buildings, where they could rent a room and live a life virtu ally free of parental or societal strictures. They came to like movies, Western-style haircuts and clothing, imported dance music, and the easy availability of the young female hostesses. In fact, the girl hostesses and their student customers were often very close in age and shared similar interests in new fashion, Western food and jazz. Had they been in a Western city, people would have assumed they were boyfriend and girlfriend out on the town for a carefree evening. Hostesses were able to earn high incomes by catering to many men, and the income of the best hostesses was equal to that of a well-paid professor. Hsu tells us that female hostesses and their male student customers, because both enjoyed strong buying power in a weak market, be came the main drivers of the city's economy during these years. They became the "new consumer’’ who was Western-oriented, young, affluent, and willing to spend. They helped to stimulate the introduction of new ideas, fashions, clothing and furniture imported from abroad. Hsu provides a number of interesting details about the lives of the hostesses. The economic rewards were high, but they entailed, besides the actual sex provided, demeaning acts such as "holdings hands, listening to bad jokes, and telling ones age". Men dissatisfied with one girl might crassly yell out that they wanted another hostess sent over. Males had all sorts of ways of taking maximum advantage of (eating, chi 吃）the poor hostesses. On the other hand, when the girls customer was an inexperienced young college boy, the girl as able to "eat" the boy. For many of the young hostesses, their best friends were the male hustlers (nanzhaodai 男招待)，who shared a similar economic position and faced the same job-related pressures. I hope that in the future Hsu will do more research into this aspect of Beiping life. Hsu describes the intellectual and cultural vibrancy of this decade. The writers and profes sors in the city began to create an industry for the appreciation of old Beijing. Hsu says that the removal of the governmental institutions, and the national gaze from Beiping, allowed its long history and many monuments to rise to the surface of public appreciation. Magazine and news paper writers started to write about the city's distinctive cuisine, its colourful colloquialisms, and its dusty temples and neighbourhood lanes (hutong 胡同）• They were creating a nostalgia for a past that was still within living memory for most citizens. They were also fostering the com mercial tourism that today is a major industry for the city. Hsu presents seventeen tables of information about wages, prices, daily costs of living and population changes during the decade. But her study is as much about Beipings social and cul tural changes as the changes in its market consumerism. She uses excellent sources, including This content downloaded from 130.209.6.61 on Fri, 26 Feb 2016 20:24:52 UTC All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

218 REVIEWS many newspapers published in the city during those years. She presents a convincing degree of detail, so that we can know, for example, the price of admission to one of the new public parks and the cost of renting an apartment, and we can trace the drop in incomes over the decade. But she never allows the documenting details to overshadow her cogent analysis of the larger forces sweeping over Beiping. Two ideas she presents gave me pause for thought. She says that when the Japanese moved into Manchuria in the early 1930s, Beiping became the centre of national resistance activities, and in that sense continued for a while longer on the national stage. This is a topic that has been explored somewhat in Chinese-language scholarship, but remains to be thoroughly looked at by Japanese and Western scholars. She also says that after the Japanese took full control of the city in 1937 and changed its name back to Beijing, the GMD government ignored the city because it did not want Chinese citizens to think about the fact that the GMD had lost the nations most iconic and historically respected city. This cut off the city from national consciousness, and what took place in the city from 1938 to 1945 remains under-researched. Hsu Hui-chi has, in sum, given us a reliable, well-documented, and intellectually engaging study of the Beiping decade of 1928 to 1937.
